findings.title: Insecure/undocumented pagination bypass gated by client-controlled query param
findings.body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` lets any authenticated caller opt into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` merely by passing a query string, combined with a permission check (`is_superuser or has_global_access`) that is evaluated per-request with no audit trail. This introduces an undocumented, non-reviewed pagination mode in a security-sensitive audit log endpoint. Combined with the negative-offset feature in OptimizedCursorPaginator, it enables bypassing normal page-boundary semantics to query negative offsets directly against the DB-backed queryset, which is unvetted and not covered by any tests added in this PR.

findings.title: Negative offset slicing can throw or produce confusing results
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, `start_offset = cursor.offset` is used directly as the slice start on a Django queryset: `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing in slices (raises `AssertionError`/`ValueError` for negative start in slicing), so this will throw at runtime rather than doing what the comment claims ("Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically"). This is untested and will blow up as soon as a negative offset cursor is supplied in combination with `enable_advanced_features=True`.

findings.title: Clamping offset to 0 silently changes pagination semantics for non-prev cursors
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` was newly introduced in `BasePaginator.get_result`. Previously `offset` (which could theoretically be negative from a malformed/garbage cursor) was used directly; this silently clamps negative offsets to 0 without raising `BadPaginationError`, unlike other paginators in this file (e.g., `OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`) which explicitly raise `BadPaginationError('Pagination offset cannot be negative')`. This creates inconsistent behavior across paginators and can mask bugs/bad input instead of surfacing an explicit error.

findings.title: Redirect-depth loop bound reduced from 10000 to 1000 without justification
findings.body: The loop bound for following redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000, and the explanatory comment about segment trees of depth up to that limit possibly not joining correctly was removed. For deep span trees exceeding 1000 redirects, segments may silently fail to merge correctly, and there is no comment warning future maintainers of this truncation behavior.

findings.title: zpopmin eviction can discard the segment's root span before flush
findings.body: When `span_count > 1000`, `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` evicts the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans without regard for whether any evicted span is the root/segment span. Since segments are scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, the root span (often the first span to start but potentially not the first to end) could be evicted, silently corrupting flushed segments with missing root-span data and no detection/logging of this data loss. There is no test covering span buffer eviction behavior at the 1000-span boundary.

findings.title: max_segment_spans config no longer enforced
findings.body: The constructor still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` but the code path in `_load_segment_data` that previously checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and skipped/logged oversized segments has been removed. Enforcement is now solely delegated to the Lua script's `zpopmin` eviction (capped at 1000), making the `max_segment_spans` parameter dead/misleading code, and removing the previous safety net against oversized segments being loaded into memory on the Python side if eviction is skipped or miscounted (e.g., due to script errors).
